changes.after: Use a calculation to keep a strip a fixed amount narrower than its parent.

before: calc() combines compatible quantities into a CSS value. In width: calc(100% - 40px), the percentage uses the containing block’s width and 40px is subtracted from that length. The result is a CSS length, not a JavaScript number.

Leave spaces around + and - in calc expressions. The parentheses contain the calculation. min(220px, 100%) chooses the smaller resulting length; max(120px, 50%) chooses the larger. Each has comma-separated alternatives. A minimum can still overflow a smaller container, so these functions do not guarantee every layout fits.

Make the strip 40px narrower than its 300px parent using calc; keep that difference when the parent changes. The supplied HTML stays in index.html; edit the CSS. The checks inspect this small page, not every possible browser or accessibility requirement.
after: `calc()` calculates a CSS value. In `calc(100% - 40px)`, `100%` means the parent’s available width here. Subtracting 40 pixels leaves a strip that is 40 pixels narrower. Keep spaces around `+` and `-`.

`min()` chooses the smaller of the sizes inside its parentheses. `max()` chooses the larger. Commas separate the choices. For example, `min(220px, 100%)` cannot ask for more than either 220 pixels or the full available width. A large minimum can still be too wide for a small box.
Keep the calculation instead of replacing it with `260px`. If the parent becomes 180 pixels wide, the strip asks for 180 − 40 = 140 pixels. The difference stays 40 pixels as the parent changes.
